reason: The sources provide ample verified claims across multiple sites to construct a surprising 45-second script about GRB 080319B.
story: In March 2008, astronomers caught a flash from the edge of the cosmos that defied belief. A dying star located 7.5 billion light-years away exploded into a gamma-ray burst designated GRB 080319B. Despite its staggering distance—halfway across the observable universe—the explosion briefly became bright enough to be seen with the unaided human eye, shining as a fifth-magnitude star in the constellation Boötes for about thirty seconds. For nearly a minute, this single dying star outshone ten million galaxies combined. Scientists discovered that this mind-bending intensity was not because it was the biggest explosion ever, but because its ultra-fast particle jet, traveling at 99.99995 percent the speed of light, was pointed directly down the barrel at Earth like a cosmic blowtorch. It is a terrifying reminder that some of the universe's most powerful weapons can shoot right at us without warning.
angle: A dying star 7.5 billion light-years away exploded so violently that it could be seen with the naked eye from Earth for about thirty seconds.

claims.claim: The explosion took place on March 19, 2008.
The burst was visible to the naked eye for approximately 30 seconds.
The object was located in the constellation Boötes.
The burst was detected by NASA's Swift satellite.
For nearly a minute, the single star was as bright as 10 million galaxies.
The extraordinary brightness arose from a jet shooting material almost directly toward Earth at 99.99995 percent the speed of light.
The distance to the burst was determined using the European Southern Observatory's Very Large Telescope.
Long-duration gamma-ray bursts are theorized to be caused by the death of very massive stars weighing up to 50 times our Sun.
Swift's X-Ray Telescope and UltraViolet/Optical Telescope were initially blinded or saturated by the brightness of the blast.
The jet directed toward Earth contained an ultra-fast component just 0.4 degrees across, contained within a wider secondary jet.
NASA's Swift satellite found a record four gamma-ray bursts on that single day.

disputed: Sources differ slightly on the exact peak magnitude, citing magnitude 5.8 (S1), dim 5th magnitude (S2, S5), and magnitude 5.3 (S7). A script should state it reached around the 5th magnitude.
